metas.name: Agriculture - Cassava
metas.note: Cassava (Manihot esculenta) can be recognised by its small, hand-shaped leaves. It can be found both in plantations as well as semi-wild in residential areas. It is most commonly seen in Lampung and Java with Lampung being the main hot spot.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Agriculture - Oil Palms
metas.note: Within Indonesia, oil palm plantations are mostly concentrated in Sumatra and Kalimantan. Palm plantations can rarely be seen in Sulawesi.

metas.name: Agriculture - Rice
metas.note: The majority of rice production is concentrated in Java, but can sometimes be found in other provinces, namely South Sulawesi and South Sumatra. They can rarely be found in other provinces as well.

metas.name: Architecture - Andesite
metas.note: Andesite, a dark, volcanic rock, is a common building material in Bali. You can often see gates, walls, and other intricately carved ornaments built from this material.

metas.name: Architecture - Bali Architecture
metas.note: Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism. The most important thing to look for are these crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali. Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too.

metas.name: Architecture - Boat Roof - Not Spiky
metas.note:
North Sumatra features similarly distinct boat-shaped roofs, however the roofs are less angled upward and they do not feature spires.

NOTE: These roofs are most commonly found near Lake Toba, due to its sacred history.

metas.name: Architecture - Boat Roof - Spiky
metas.note: West Sumatra features these distinct boat-shaped roofs.

metas.name: Architecture - Flat Tiles
metas.note: The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different. The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.

metas.name: Architecture - Horny Roof
metas.note:
Roofs with gable horns can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi, Riau and Central and South Kalimantan.

NOTE: Horned roofs are often found with Bugis roofs in South Sulawesi. Use this tip along with other clues to determine which region you are in.

metas.name: Architecture - Java Roof
metas.note:
Tiled roofs are most commonly found on the island of Java, and sometimes nearby regions such as southern Sumatra, the Lesser Sunda Islands, and South Kalimantan.

NOTE: The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different. The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.

metas.name: Architecture - Malay Canopies
metas.note: In the regions of Sumatra and Kalimantan that lie opposite Malaysia, many buildings have metal canopies with curved ends. These canopies are often blue or red.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Architecture - Nias Roof
metas.note: Steeply pitched roofs made of palm tree leaves can sometimes be seen on Nias Island, south west of North Sumatra.

metas.name: Architecture - Sheet Roofs
metas.note: Plain sheet metal roofs are more commonly found toward the north, where tiled roofs are not found. They are most commonly found on Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra.

metas.name: Architecture - South Sula House
metas.note:
These horizontal slots inside the triangles of the roofs are almost unique to Southern Sulawesi.

NOTE: They can rarely be found in East Kalimantan and West Nusa.

metas.name: Architecture - Sumba Roof
metas.note: You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.

metas.name: Architecture - Tongkonan
metas.note: A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs. The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.

metas.name: Architecture - Wooden Chips Roof
metas.note: On Kalimantan, you can find these unique roofs made out of wooden chips.

metas.name: Car Meta - Gen 3 Antenna
metas.note: Generation 3 antenna coverage is most commonly found on Java, but can very rarely be seen on Bali in and around Denpasar. It is most commonly seen in East Java, as most of the antenna coverage in the west has been overwritten by Generation 4.

metas.name: Car Meta - Gen 3 Black
metas.note: Black Generation 3 coverage can be found almost everywhere in Indonesia, but is most common in Sulawesi.

metas.name: Car Meta - Jagasatru Car
metas.note: A black cab with men sitting in the truck bed can be seen near Jagasatru on Bali.

metas.name: Car Meta - Wooden Plank Car
metas.note: A white SUV with black bars and a wooden plank on the roof can rarely be seen in eastern Bali.

metas.name: Coverage Meta - Pink Air
metas.note: In some of the Generation 4 coverage in the city of Batam, a purple tint and a black blurred object can be seen. Although this camera glitch is most commonly found in Batam, you may spot it in nearby regions such as North Sumatra, around Medan. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Cigarette Blocks
metas.note: Central Sulawesi features these unique bollards that are painted black on the bottom, white in the middle, and yellow on the top.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Even Pole
metas.note: Indonesia uses two types of pole tops: even and uneven. This refers to the bar that holds the insulators and whether it is symmetrical to the pole itself. Knowing where even and uneven poles are most commonly found is useful for region guessing.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Green Bridge
metas.note: Green paint can often be seen on the side of bridges in South and Central Kalimantan.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Indented Pole
metas.note: Poles with an indent on both sides are found in West Java, Jakarta, and Banten.

metas.name: Infrastructure - North Sumatra Pole
metas.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Nusa Pole
metas.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands ('Nusas'), you can find poles with an extra long support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Pole Tape
metas.note: You can often see thin, black poles next to regular poles near the East Peninsula of Central Sulawesi. Two pieces of tape can be seen near the top of the poles, usually light blue and green. These can rarely be seen in northern South East Sulawesi.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Rectangle Attachment
metas.note: Bali features both even and uneven poles, as well as the Lesser Sunda island variants. You can also find this unique rectangle attachment on the pole tops in Bali.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Sulawesi Fences
metas.note: These painted fences are typically found on Sulawesi. They will be mostly painted white with blue or red.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Surabaya Pavement
metas.note: Pavement made out of bricks like this is found in East Java, particularly around Surabaya

metas.name: Infrastructure - Trapezoid Pole
metas.note: Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Triangle Attachment
metas.note:
You can find these poles with a triangle attachment under the horizontal bar in the following regions.

NOTE: This does not apply to stacked poles.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Trident Pole
metas.note: Trident style pole tops are most commonly found in Central Java and Yogyakarta, and rarely in South and West Kalimantan, and North Sumatra and Riau.

metas.name: Infrastructure - Uneven Pole
metas.note: Indonesia uses two types of pole tops: even and uneven. This refers to the bar that holds the insulators and whether it is symmetrical to the pole itself. Knowing where even and uneven poles are most commonly found is useful for region guessing.

metas.name: Landscape - Dryness
metas.note:
The Nusas typically look drier than other regions in Indonesia. The islands get especially dry towards the east, especially in Generation 3. Vegetation tends to look less tropical, but instead more brown with a lack of leaves. Sumba Island is also the driest of the Nusas.

NOTE: While less common, other regions such as Java can look similarly dry. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

metas.name: Landscape - Lake Toba
metas.note: The region around Lake Toba, in North Sumatra, can be recognized by mountains surrounding the lake and Samosir Island in the middle. Overcast coverage is also common for the region.

metas.name: Landscape - Palu Bay
metas.note: Palu Bay is a unique slightly north-west facing bay just north of Palu city, which features mountains to the west of the bay, and a flat, more urbanised landscape to the east.

metas.name: Landscape - Red Soil
metas.note: Red soil can often be found on Batam and the Bangka Belitung islands, located east of mainland Sumatra.

metas.name: Landscape - Savannah
metas.note:
This savannah landscape is occasionally seen on North Sumba.

NOTE: In Generation 3, you will always see a white car.

metas.name: Misc - Christianity
metas.note: Indonesia is religiously a Muslim majority country, so seeing churches, and other Christian signs, is a good clue for these regions.

metas.name: Vegetation - Areca
metas.note: Areca palms (Areca catechu) are most prominent in western Sumatra; however they can also be seen elsewhere less commonly. They can be recognised by their relatively short and thick leaves.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Coastal She-Oak
metas.note: Coastal she-oak (Casuarina equisetifolia) can be found along the coast throughout much of the country, but particularly in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Java. Their leaves resemble the needles of pine trees, but are noticeably longer. Another species of she-oak can be found in mountainous regions throughout the country.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Coconut
metas.note: Coconut palms (Cocos nucifera) can be found in many regions throughout Indonesia, but are most abundant along the coast, especially in western Sumatra, southern Java, northern Sulawesi and North Maluku.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Footstool Palm
metas.note: Footstool palm (Saribus rotundifolius) has fan-shaped leaves similar to those of Palmyra palm; however the crown is more open, the leaves are thinner and the palm itself is usually taller. It can be found most notably in Sulawesi and more rarely in other parts of the country.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Gebang Palm
metas.note: Gebang palm (Corypha utan) can at first glance look similar to both Palmyra and footstool palm due to its fan-shaped leaves, however the leaves are noticeably larger, stiffer and more upright in contrast to the round crown shape of both Palmyra and footstool palm. Unlike most palms, the gebang palm will only flower once at the end of its life in a dramatic gesture where the leaves wither away and it shoots one large inflorescence into the heavens before it dies. It is found mainly in the east of the country, namely Sulawesi and the Nusas.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Milkweed
metas.note: Giant milkweed (Calotropis gigantea) is a small shrub with thick round leaves and pale flowers. It can be found in dry regions of Indonesia, namely the Nusas and parts of Java and Sulawesi.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Palmyra
metas.note: Palmyra palms (Borassus flabellifer) can be recognised by their fan-shaped leaves and dense round crowns. Compared to footstool palm, the crown is more dense, the leaves are heavier and the palm itself is usually shorter. It is found in dry parts of the country, namely the Nusas and South Sulawesi.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - Sumatran Pine
metas.note: Sumatran pines (Pinus merkusii) in Indonesia can be found in a few pockets across the country, notable areas include North Sumatra and Java. They can be recognised by having long needles for leaves, but be careful not to confuse them with she-oak, which has even longer leaves.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group

metas.name: Vegetation - White Leadtree
metas.note: White leadtree (Leucaena leucocephala) can be recognised by its delicate featherlike (bipinnate) leaves. Fruits are often also visible in the form of legume pods. It can be found mainly in the Nusas as well as a few other dry areas of the country.
metas.footer: Source: Real Meta Research Group
